en: Preface to the Yongjia Song of Realizing the Way by Nanmingquan:
I have heard that the Tathāgata well protects and mindfully sustains all bodhisattvas with his heart, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas with the Dharma.
That which the mind points toward cannot be encompassed by words; that which the Dharma transmits cannot be exhausted by thought.
Both words and thought are merely various delusions. That which transcends words and thought is likewise so. Neither identical nor separate, all things are equal.
One does not fall into non-existence, nor does one cling to existence. When both words and thought are forgotten, the nature of the mind and the Dharma are attained. Indeed, it is thus.
The Dharma is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It stands in opposition to objects; the mind has no fixed characteristics, yet it manifests in accordance with phenomena.

Therefore, it does not come from the past (*pūrvānta*) nor go to the future (*aparānta*). In the present, it is like a turning wheel or a flowing stream—neither flowing nor turning, yet neither remaining stationary.
To not remain stationary is to have no location. To have no location is to be nowhere not located. This is true permanence.
Yet those who are ignorant do not understand this; they perceive the Tathāgata through form and seek the Tathāgata through sound—is this not utterly erroneous?
Master Yongjia’s *Song of Enlightenment* is profound in its realization of the Way. However, the Way has nothing to do with being "realized.
Yet Yongjia speaks at length, even to the point of debating with worldly people. Is he perhaps constrained by words?
How profound this is! Only the Tathāgata does not weary of the world while entering nirvāṇa; he does not depart from words and letters while abiding in liberation;
he does not sever afflictions while flowing forth all true suchness and bodhi. Yongjia’s realization was precisely of this nature.
Formerly, when Chan Master Nanming Quan resided at Qianqing, he further composed a verse on the *Song of Realizing the Way*, forming three [sections].
One hundred and twenty chapters. Alas! To bring forth the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, enabling all people to behold its shores and trace its currents;
to ceaselessly maintain mindfulness, to remain unattached to signs, and not to look outward for causes and conditions;
to universally employ my own awakening to gladden the hearts of the multitude—how magnificent this is! Beholding these verses, I can do nothing but lament my own madness.
Thus, he composed this preface:
On the seventh day of the seventh month in the tenth year of the Xīníng era (the Dīngyí year), by Wú Yōng Tiānyòng of Kuòcāng.
Preface to the *Song of Realizing the Way* by the Chan Master Zhēnjué of Yǒngjiā.
The Śramaṇa Fashui of Qianqing Mountain continues the verse on the Song of Realizing the Way.
He sings this melody: At the assembly of Nirvāṇa, he was personally entrusted with these words; The golden-colored dhūta monk laughs without ceasing.
A few peaks of green mountains face his thatched cottage.
Do you not see? What manner of countenance is this? To deliberate or reflect is to be separated by mountains of chaos.
From this point on, the words from outside Caoxi’s gate shall continue as before to drift and fall among the people of the world.
The man of the Way who has severed study and is non-active dwells in leisure; like the tracks of clouds and the gait of cranes, what reliance has he? Deep in spring, the secluded birds do not return;
by the crags, the clusters of flowers bloom and fall of their own accord.
Do not eliminate delusive thoughts, nor seek the truth; both truth and delusion are like dust in a mirror.
When empty space is shattered and light and shadow are severed, only then do you see the person of original nature.
The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; these two designations are established by convention according to their respective origins.
When the four seas are tranquil and clear and the seasonal rains are sufficient, there is no need for the rustic elders to offer congratulations on the peace and prosperity of the realm.

The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. If one realizes that the Dharma-body has neither interior nor exterior, even the scabies-infested dog and the mud-smeared pig will know it together.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have never met with it.
The Dharmakāya is fully awakened, devoid of a single thing; it is as pure as a cloudless sky, free from even a speck of mist.
Recalling the events of that day at Vulture Peak, I take up my staff and tread upon the withered flowers along the spring path.
The fundamental source and original nature is the true, heavenly Buddha; eyes like blue lotuses, teeth like white jade.
If you do not recognize the Compassionate Honored One, you must depart in haste—turn your head, and the hawk has already flown to Silla.
The five aggregates are like floating clouds, empty in their coming and going; they appear substantial yet are not real.
A single gust of the western wind sweeps them away without a trace, leaving ten thousand miles of mountains and rivers shared with the clear sun.
The bubbles of the three poisons emerge and submerge in vain; their arising and ceasing leave no trace and cannot be fathomed. Do not say that the names and forms of these bubbles are different;
a thousand waves and ten thousand ripples all flow toward the same source.
Realizing the true mark, one transcends all subtlety; it is not in the east, nor is it in the west. Best of all is the third and second month in Jiangnan:
plucking flowers in the warm breeze as the partridges cry.
There is no dharma of a person; it is simply this person who says that this year has been truly impoverished. With every glance, there is nowhere to rely;
even outside the Diamond Gate, resentment still lingers.
In a single instant, the karma of Avīci is extinguished; do not say that good and evil take different paths.
You must know that the nature of sin is like frost and snow—once the sun of wisdom rises, not a single trace remains.
If one deceives sentient beings with false speech, by what means can one oneself attain liberation? This mind is like a solitary boat throughout the day;
it seeks only that all living beings may avoid falling into ruin.
One has invited for oneself the punishment of having one's tongue plucked out for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; how could such immense kindness ever be easily repaid?
Facing this, I feel pity instead for the wanderer who wastes his time and light away, never looking back.
Suddenly awakened and realized, one immediately forgets the trap; as before, the eyebrows remain above the eyes. What need is there to speak of the higher mechanism?
When hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps.
The Tathāgata-dhyāna must be realized through subtle awakening; it is quiescent, unconditioned, and transcends the four propositions.
Though a round fan may be used to represent the lunar orb, a swift falcon does not strike at a rabbit by the hedge.

The essence of the myriad practices of the six perfections is perfectly complete; within this true essence, there is no need to distinguish between sameness and difference. Like the moonlight upon ten thousand waters, it comes and goes as it pleases;
yet the heart of heaven remains a single, radiant moon.
Within the dream, the six realms of existence are clearly manifest; suffering and joy intersect without a moment’s pause.
If one wishes to escape the ocean of birth and death within saṃsāra, one must look from the Big Dipper toward the Southern Star.
After awakening, all is empty and void; there is not even a "great chiliocosm. Only now do I believe that what I previously held was but self-imposed bondage.
If one now wishes to recognize original emptiness, the green mountains beyond the gate lean against the vast expanse of space.
Without sin or merit, delusion and truth are both discarded. Like the bright moon at the end of autumn, it cannot be compared even to its fullness;
though Mañjuśrī wields his sword, he still does not perceive it—how could birth and death ever reach its presence?
There is neither loss nor gain; what further doubt could there be? Since time immemorial, Buddhas and patriarchs have never known it; north, south, east, and west, it is uninterrupted.
Niaoke merely blew on a tuft of cloth.
Within the nature of quiescent extinction, do not seek or inquire. To sit and sever the peaks—those who pass through find it difficult. Do not be surprised that no guests arrive at the empty hall;
from the beginning, outsiders have never been permitted to look within.
Lately, the dusty mirror has never been polished; with mental defilements as its condition, it has gradually grown dark and black.
When a drop of divine ointment brings forth a hall of cool clarity, one finally believes that the numinous light is not transmitted from without.
Today, one must clearly analyze and discern; how could one begrudge the effort to transcend worldly sentiments?
When drifting clouds disperse and the solitary moon rises, the ten-thousandfold world-system is illuminated all at once.
Who is without thought? All thoughts are true. If one realizes this truth, yet has not yet emerged from the dust of the world, it is the constant rule to leave the boat once the shore is reached.
Why need one further inquire of those at the river's head?
Who is without birth? Birth is delusion. When delusion arises without root, it is the true mark (*dharmatā*). One night, the waters of Caoxi flowed upstream;
ordinary people are limited by non-birth, following along with the waves.
If in reality there is neither arising nor non-arising, how could the arising of arising differ from non-arising? At the time of non-arising, not a single thing exists;
if one wishes to know non-arising, all phenomena are it.
Summon the wooden man of the mechanism and ask him: this principle has from the beginning never belonged to knowledge.
If you claim that non-knowledge is the true Way, then in the autumn wind the palace halls will see the millet stalks drooping.
Seeking to attain Buddhahood through the application of effort—when will it ever be accomplished? Without anything to realize and nothing to cultivate, merit naturally endures for a long time.
Behold the void filling the space before you; how could it be grasped or manipulated by human hands?
Release the four great elements; sit alone and walk alone without hindrance. Tearing up your mat, leisurely drag it away and sleep facing the sun.
With what mind would you seek further to transcend the three realms?
Do not grasp at things; to be fussy and restrictive is to commit a great error. If you wish to use the mind and will to study practice, [you are like] the great void.
How could one fail to develop the horns of wisdom?
Amidst the nature of quiescent extinction, one follows the rhythm of eating and drinking; without thought or deliberation, one blends with the flow of time.
Having once partaken of a single grain of rice from the family field, one remains satiated even until now, never ceasing.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all are empty. The nature of dependent origination and its cessation are fundamentally the same.
To seek a substantial reality while wishing to abandon dependent arising is like asking for the north while walking toward the east.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment; there is not a single thing that can be altered or corrected. The mountain colors leaning against the eaves are as verdant as clouds;
the flower branches emerging from the railing bear the fragrance of dew.
This is a definitive teaching; do not harbor doubt. To directly accept it is already late. What did Xiangyan accomplish on that day?
Striking the bamboo was merely said to be the highest capacity.
It manifests the true vehicle and is not false or deceptive; it encompasses all the infinite meanings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Firm and dense, it is like gold refined a hundred times;
though one might test it with a hard hammer and fierce flames, it remains unyielding.
Some people are unwilling to let their minds rest as they investigate; thoughts and phrases race across them in a thousand myriad forms.
Yet the flower branches in the garden, regardless of whether they are short or long, are treated with equal grace by the Azure Emperor’s spring breeze.
Directly cutting through to the root is the seal of the Buddhas; in the space of a flash of lightning or a gust of wind.
Hurry back home without looking back; in an instant the cold sun will sink behind the western mountains.
I am unable to pluck leaves or seek out branches; though I turn them over and examine them repeatedly, what can I find?
Alas for the wandering traveler who pursues fragrant blossoms, unaware that the dust of the mundane world corrodes their beauty.
The mani-jewel is originally without flaw; it transcends both the refined and the coarse. Under a bright moon and a clear breeze on last year’s night, a single sail flew past Lake Dongting.
People do not recognize it; from immeasurable kalpas past until this very day, let go of your skin-sack and look closely. There is no need for—
Seeking it outwardly in emptiness, one finds it personally within the Tathāgatagarbha. Do you wish to recognize the Tathāgatagarbha? A few cups of sour wine and cold tea;
the wind is swift upon the long river, and the flower-crests are many.

The six modes of spiritual function are both empty and non-empty; whether among sages or ordinary beings, their essential nature is no different. When the Gate of Non-duality opens, one may go and return as one pleases;
what need is there to further consult Vimalakīrti?
A single orb of light, neither form nor non-form—how difficult it is for Aniruddha to perceive! Who has ever seen its true essence?
The wind is high, and heaven and earth are cold with snow and frost.

The five eyes are purified; differences return to sameness. Ten thousand distinctions and a thousand variations are ultimately empty. Who could know the infinite events of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust?
They are like viewing an *āmra* fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
To attain the five powers is true cultivation. Departing further and further, one long relies upon the flow of the noble path; proceeding directly toward Bodhicitta, it is no mere mat.
What demon or outsider would dare to raise its head?
Only through direct realization can it be known; it is difficult to fathom. A single point of solitary luminosity is like the great sun;
the blind do not know where its light resides, as they sit with bowed heads, coldly contemplating in the dark.
It is not difficult to see one's form when looking in a mirror; though the features may appear similar, they are not the reality.
If you wish to recognize your original host from years past, lift your eyebrows this very day.
In the water, they grasp at the moon, competing to seize it; yet where has the true moon ever been in the water?
If only the frantic delusions of the foolish monkeys could cease, then the Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji Rivers would all flow unimpeded at once.
I always travel alone. Having passed through Tongguan, I inquire about the journey: a path dense with trees where no one arrives;
green moss grows upon the golden palace. I always walk alone;
from now on, do not seek other gateways. Why speak of Hanshan’s love for distant travels? Now—
Forgetting the path by which one came;
those who have attained travel together upon the road to nirvana. Behold it, bright and clear—do not obstruct it! From antiquity to the present, its treading has never ceased.
O traveler, do not say that setting foot upon it is difficult.
The tune is ancient and the spirit is pure; the wind naturally rises high. If one stumbles by even a hair’s breadth, it will not be permitted.
Suddenly encountering the right moment atop the peak of wondrous heights, one does not become a companion to the white clouds.
His countenance was haggard and his bones were firm; people paid him no heed. How could an ordinary person who judges by outward signs easily fathom him?
Zisi Gong did not know the taste of wild herbs, so he vainly galloped his team of four horses to the gate.
The destitute Śākya son continues the true tradition; the style of the Tathāgatas of the three periods is identical. Do not be surprised that his entire being possesses nothing;
his household goods have been empty from the very beginning.
The mouth professes poverty, yet the mind is radiant and clear. Dwelling neither in city nor mountain forest, one wears this mother-born tattered cloth robe;
through many kalpas of cosmic conflagration, it remains ever thus.
In truth, it is this body that is poor; the Way is not poor. With nothing in my bag to pass through the green years, I tell you, people of the world:
cease from grasping at appearances. Each time it is lifted up, it is fresh once more.
Being poor, one’s body is constantly clad in coarse, threadbare garments; when meeting others, do not laugh at such tattered rags. At times, shake them out and hold them up idly;
this is superior to wearing a robe of brocade and embroidery while remaining empty within.
The Way is the priceless treasure within the mind-treasury; it is difficult to compare with anything in the mundane or supramundane worlds. Look directly before the mountain of the five aggregates;
once you are pointed to it, it does not come from ten thousand miles away.
Priceless jewel, the jewel of jewels—searching throughout the dragon palaces, it cannot be found.
Even if a shipowner possessed skillful expedients, to open his mouth to deliberate upon it would surely lead to vexation.
Its use is inexhaustible; how could anything surpass it? From antiquity to the present, it flows on like a surging wave.
That the power of compassionate vows has permeated things to this extent—this fragrant rice of Vaiśālī was not so much as this.
Benefiting beings by manifesting forms according to need, he never begrudges his power; it is like a dragon king sending down rain:
as soon as he raises his intent, wind and clouds spread across the world, so that there is no flower or tree that remains untouched.
The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within the essence; this essence has never been dual from the beginning.
If one remains free from seeking within the self-nature, the myriad kinds of names and phrases are not the true meaning.
The eight liberations, the six supernormal powers, and the seal of the mind-ground—mud, water, and space have no equal in their threefold function.
Only where the Iron Ox once stood, to the east of the Bamboo Grove and west of the Stone Bridge.

The superior person makes a single decisive resolution and understands all things; their momentum is like a collapsing mountain, leaving nothing behind. How could they be like those who seek a sword by marking the spot on a boat?
The boat has moved, yet they still guard the bow.
Those of middling and inferior capacity have heard much but lack faith, for they have been away from home for many years. I urge you to cease seeking from this day forth;
you shall naturally possess precious wealth that fills your native land.
Simply untie the soiled garment from within your own breast; this robe has been priceless from the very beginning.
Now that the thread has frayed and its true nature is fully revealed, do not laboriously search for seams or gaps.
Who can boast of their diligence to others? Such people harbor a mind of grasping and rejecting, defiled by passion.
Where the flowers bloom within the Peach Blossom Spring, there is spring of its own accord, without waiting for the eastern breeze.
Though others slander me, my mind remains at peace. All speech is but the sound of the wind; wooden men, flowers, and birds have long met one another.
If they were without sentience, they would not be startled.
Let others be "not so"; "not so" is also so. When has "not so" ever reached the definitive meaning? With what could the definitive meaning be pointed out?
Deep in spring, flowers fall upon the mossy ground.
To set fire to the heavens merely exhausts oneself; how could the vast, azure sky ever give rise to affliction?
If you unite yourself with empty space, this is the Tathāgata’s true path.
Hearing this, it was as if I had drunk nectar; a single drop can cause ten thousand ailments to vanish.
Reclining high upon my mountain hall in tranquil leisure, I leave the passing of today and tomorrow to fate.
Dissolving away, one enters suddenly into the inconceivable; now there is no need for further dissolution.
Directly and clearly, extract it with vigor—several stalks of tall bamboo, a single hall of wind.
Contemplating harsh words: if one realizes that there is ultimately no speech, the principle is impartial. How many times have the river winds blown for days on end?
Yet we have never heard of a fishing boat being submerged. This is merit.
The sword of wisdom is wielded personally against the thief of afflictions; once the smoke and dust are swept away, one returns. A single color.
Every single fragrance is a pure land;

this very thing becomes my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). With a mind of forbearance like an illusion, it is stirred yet leaves no trace. Datta personally received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*);
how could I engrave this upon my bones to repay such kindness?
Do not give rise to enmity or affection because of slander; strive only to recognize those on the path of Caoxi.
Having once crossed the Flowing Sands before the dawn, they remain until now with their faces covered in dust.
What manifests the power of the patience of non-arising? Non-arising is self-realized, and even that patience is forgotten. Where does one return as one grows old with the passing years?
Every land and every atom is one’s native home.
The fundamental principle is also pervasive; it is the true secret instruction. In years past at Magadha, he once spoke of it:
Mañjuśrī struck down the old Vimalakīrti, and to this day there is no way to clear his name.
The teaching is likewise pervasive; its meanings are immeasurable. It is proclaimed in accordance with the capacities of those who are to be inspired.
If one can reach the fundamental root through words, one will realize that the yellow leaves used to stop a child’s crying are but empty fabrications.
Samādhi and prajñā are perfectly luminous, not lingering in emptiness; drifting up and down, there is no place to be found.
Sometimes they come of their own accord with the white clouds; last night, they followed the bright moon away.
It is not that I alone have now attained realization; when has it ever fallen within the scope of my vision or knowledge?
To say "I exist" is simply to remain unenlightened; to say "I do not exist" is even more deluded.
The essence of all Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is identical. This essence has been uninterrupted from the very beginning. Desiring to know this essence, I proclaim it for you:
the fisherman stands smiling upon the bank of reeds.
The lion’s roar resounds with perfect fullness; its power, penetrating the most profound and subtle, remains entirely intact.
Sentient beings, shrouded in darkness, receive the dawn of enlightenment—everlasting like the thunder of spring that breaks forth across the heavens.
Fearlessly proclaimed, without deviation; both ordinary and sage beings are like those with blurred vision.
Opening a path through the thicket of thorns, let us proceed together to the King of Dharma’s palace.

When the hundred beasts heard this, their brains were all split open; it was like when the hosts of Māra hear the True Teaching—they return in grief and terror, losing their former appearance, unaware that from the beginning there is neither birth nor extinction.
The fragrant elephant rushes about, having lost its majesty; the realization of the nature by those of the Two Vehicles is just like this.
Not knowing that afflictions are themselves bodhi, they seek nirvana for themselves and loathe birth-and-death.
The devas and nāgas listen in silence, giving rise to joy; all living beings from this point on find their refuge. The secluded crags remain silent and do not look back;
he has instead returned to the human world, wearing tattered robes.

Wandering through rivers and seas, he has exhausted the very sources of their depths; yet his aspiration remains. Possessing a golden pitcher that surpasses precious jewels, the Dragon King need not worry in vain.
Traversing mountains and rivers, his staff once cleared the mist from the byways. Who knows today of those matters of yesteryear? At times...
Leaning idly before my thatched cottage, I seek teachers and inquire after the Way to practice Zen. Why did Xuansha not cross the ridge? Alas for you people of today who deceive yourselves;
though you strike your own foreheads until they bleed, you still do not realize it.
Since I recognized the path of Caoxi, my alms-bowl and needle-case have been open day and night.
If you see those who were chasing after me in years past, tell them that Old Lu awaits your arrival.

He fully understood that birth and death are not interconnected; having realized that death and life have neither going nor staying, Bāṣpa still possesses the legacy of that day—lifting his twin golden feet toward the Śāla trees.
Walking is also Zen; it does not fall into the middle or the two extremes. Master Xiong’er once leaked this secret:
"Carrying a single shoe alone, he went to the Western Heaven.
Sitting is also Zen; it is neither raised nor sunk—how could it be a mere blank stillness? The traveler does not realize that spring has already passed, having mistakenly listened...
The oriole becomes the cuckoo;
whether speaking or silent, moving or still, its essence remains at ease. Though myriad circumstances come to invade it, it remains utterly unmoved;
having put on those old straw sandals of yore, the protective talisman is entirely useless.
Even if one encounters a sharp blade, one remains ever serene; having realized the emptiness of the aggregates, the body is already forgotten.
Do not be surprised by the absence of anxiety or fear when facing peril—such a person is one whose family lineage is identical to that of the Patriarchs.
Even if it were potent poison, it would remain tranquil; I have once obtained the Golden Man’s secret instruction for protecting life. I have only heard that frozen water fears the spring breeze;
I have yet to see turbid mud defile the bright moon.
My Master beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; spreading his hair upon the mud, his resolve did not waver.
Today the Tathāgata has appeared once more; do not say that there is no longer one like him was then.
For many kalpas you were once the Rishi Kṣāntivādin; your nature was like space, free from any thought of anger.
Though you were mocked as you held a sharp-edged sword that lacked a blade, you, King of Songs, did not cease your lamentation.
How many times have I been born? Through the long, dark night, I have wandered aimlessly. Day after day, changing heads and faces, I have forgotten my original name from years past.
How many times have I died?
Piles of bones as high as mountains still do not cease. Should I encounter a rustic elder before these mountains, I shall move with the slow, croaking steps of a frog.
They do not return to their native villages;
birth and death drift on endlessly without fixed rest. Greed and delusion are like wine that intoxicates one so as to be difficult to sober up; in profound darkness, they forget the road home.
Floating away and sinking down, they are like duckweed upon the water.
Since attaining sudden enlightenment to non-arising, the nature-seed has been cultivated until hatred and love are severed; names and forms are cut off down to the finest hair.
The ocean is vast and the mountains high—those of ordinary mind do not understand.
Amidst all honors and insults, what cause for sorrow or joy? Like a stone encountering spring that does not change with the season, I ask you:
of whom do the blossoming and falling of the peach and plum trees before the courtyard belong?

Entering the deep mountains, he finds joy in nourishing his sickly countenance from dawn until dusk. If those of this age wish to understand the intent within the crags, they should observe how the secluded birds occasionally return with the severed clouds.

Dwelling in an araṇya, far removed from the clamor of the dust, those who seek true stillness should look at how he lets his mind-monkey roam all day long; how could this compare [to worldly pursuits]?
Deeply dwelling to tame the horse of the mind, amidst towering peaks and secluded depths beneath long pines; with a single thought stilled, ten thousand anxieties turn to ash.
A single path through the dust leads to the mountain summit—who can understand the joy of stealing a moment’s leisure to come here?
Leisurely and at ease, I sit in the dwelling of a wild monk. When weary, I sleep; when thirsty, I drink tea. With the passing of summer and the arrival of winter, what else is there?
A single cloud-like robe is my way of life.
Secluded in tranquil retreat, truly serene and carefree; In the dense concealment of practice, no trace is revealed.
The thousand eyes open at once, with nowhere to seek; Casually, one meets again beneath the gate.
Awakening is immediate realization: at noon, the third watch, midnight, or dawn, as soon as the peach blossoms fall, the apricot flowers bloom.
Only then does one believe that from the beginning there has never been anything lacking.
Without applying effort—desiring to know this "effortlessness" is just like the wind: without anger, without joy, and without mental intention, it blows away the sand.
The drumming mist fills the clear sky;
all conditioned phenomena are not the same. One should purify the source of the mind to seek liberation;
like dewdrops or bubbles sinking in an instant, all things in this floating life are thus.

Giving with attachment gives rise to the merit of rebirth in heaven; one may pass one’s time at will within jade palaces and flowered terraces. Do not speak of how sweeping away stones can endure for long;
compared to the state of non-arising, even that is but a moment.
It is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void; that arrow has no way to settle within the sky.
One must seek the true nature to advance toward Bodhi, lest one be forced to change faces and heads within the three miserable realms.
When one's power and vigor are exhausted, one gradually becomes frail and leaning, like a celestial being who perceives the five signs of decay;
only then does one grow weary and grieve over the suffering of the prison of saṃsāra, no longer resembling the time of true joy in the pleasure gardens.
The arrow falls back down; it rests only when its momentum is exhausted. The waves of consciousness drift like scattered bubbles, once again pulled away by the weight of habitual karma.
Reaching this point, how could one ever attain true freedom?
It brings about an unfavorable rebirth; when the cause is not upright, the fruit will surely be so. In practicing dāna, one must ensure the purity of the three wheels.
Though sin and merit are potent, what can be done against them?
How can they compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark? If you wish to know the true mark, it is truly markless.
When spring arrives, the hidden birds sing all day long; when the moon rises, the fisherman’s boat is launched throughout the night.

Transcending directly into the stage of the Tathāgata, one realizes it all at once; what need is there for the full moon’s countenance? It is like the day a fish transforms into a dragon at the Dragon Gate:
after a single roll of thunder, its trace can no longer be found.
If you only grasp the root, you will need no further exertion of lips or tongue all day long. Once satisfied and full to bursting, all matters come to rest;
let others laugh as you remain free from calculation.
Do not worry about the end; the world is infinite, yet it is but a single pinch of dust. This broken-legged cauldron needs no borrowing—it boils the porridge.
Brewing tea, I personally carry it forth;
like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon, essence and function intermingle with brilliant clarity. Those with eyes cannot glimpse even a semblance;
only those without a [discursive] mind perceive the original perfection.
I now unravel this wish-fulfilling jewel; it radiates forth a cold brilliance of thousands of myriad fathoms. Beings of the four births and six classes may seek from it as they please;
while worlds have their limits, this is inexhaustible.
Benefiting self and others never ceases; the water of compassion and the flower of the mind bloom at midnight.
Unable to remain within the golden halls and jade chambers, he dons fur and wears horns once more.
The river moon shines; this is the most essential tradition of the patch-robed monks. In the stillness of night, with whom can one discuss this mind?
Among the chaotic mountains, a solitary monkey occasionally calls.
The pine wind blows; brushing against the face, it is a ceaseless, whistling sound. Beneath the roots, the lingzhi fungus has entered into the subtle mystery. Coming and going...
How many woodcutters know this?
Through the long night and the clear sky, what is there to do? When walking, walk; when sitting, sit. Horses grow horns and jars grow roots;
I shall never lightly reveal it for you.
The Buddha-nature, the pearl of precepts, the seal of the mind-ground—pervading heaven and earth, leaving nothing out. Throughout the vast, teeming world, all possess it equally;
who says it is transmitted only by the blue-eyed barbarian?
Mist, dew, clouds, and rosy mists are the garments upon the body; the substance of these garments has never had a separate name. Cease saying that not a single thing was brought forth;
the great earth, mountains, and rivers were all created by me.
The Dragon-Taming Alms Bowl: its substance is firm and solid; when spread out, it fills all space, leaving nothing to escape. It has once held the myriad worlds of the great trichiliocosm;
it fears not the ten-thousand-fathom heights that grasp the clouds.

The tiger’s staff is released; its resonance echoes through the distant void. It divides and battles as it flies amidst the soaring peaks. One does not realize that the enemy and the kin are of one essence;
in vain do they boast of the traces left behind at Mount Wangwu.
The two-pronged golden rings ring out clearly; this very perfection of penetration serves as the guiding compass.
Only when you see the true dwelling place of Avalokiteśvara will you know it does not reside on Mount Potalaka.
This is not a matter of displaying forms or engaging in empty affairs; it is intended to cause one to turn back toward the source through hearing.
Suddenly, when seeking its trace at the place of listening, no footprint is found. Look further at the ancient model of Kāśyapa.
The Tathāgata’s precious staff follows his own tracks; it can sever the nets and snares for all living beings.
Though the two-pronged form with six rings is well-expressed, if one does not recognize its total manifestation, it is not enough.
Do not seek the True. To seek the True is to have distinctions between the distant and the near. Try placing gold dust in both eyes;
though precious, how could it fail to obstruct one? Do not sever the delusive.
Delusion and the source of the True share one and the same mark. Have you not seen those playing in the tide on the river? You have never heard...
Attachment is the water; aversion is the wave.
To fully realize that these two phenomena are empty and signless is to forget both the real and the false, such that the false becomes the real. If one claims it is real, it is still false;
if one forgets both real and false, it causes even greater sorrow.
Without marks, without emptiness, and without non-emptiness; without going, without coming, and without a place of rest. Beneath the pines, the clear breeze sweeps away all the moss;
the thatched hut remains as before within the white clouds.
This is the true mark of the Tathāgata; its brilliance cannot be matched by the moon or the color of reeds. At that time, the Universal Eye had no place to seek it;
last night, it stayed with the rain in the cold stream.
The mirror of the mind is bright, its radiance reaching both near and far; it is difficult to compare even to the rising of the brilliant sun in the sky.
A single expanse of cold light remains profound and still, yet from it the great chiliocosm of sand-grain worlds arises.
The mirror is unimpeded; it transcends the finest hair’s breadth. Ten thousand couches and a thousand forms remain mutually unknown.
After the person has departed from within the silent radiance—who is this whose nose resembles his eyebrows?
Vastly open and crystal clear, it pervades the entire realm of sand-grains; meeting thus, it is entirely not the face of former days.
Do not say that from the beginning there has been no place to seek it; sometimes it wags its tail and ascends South Mountain.
Within the manifestation of the myriad phenomena, every dharma is neither empty nor substantial;
names and forms are fundamentally unarisen—just as the lion formed by many hairs is complete within a single hair.
A single orb of light is neither internal nor external; nearby it has no shape, afar it has no boundary.
Children, not recognizing its emptiness, call it vast and remote, yet claim it is round like the lunar disc.
Vastly open and empty; he is enticed by Māra. He claims that all things are utterly non-existent. The road ahead is still long, yet the sun has already set.
How pitiable, standing alone like a dog that has lost its home.
To deny cause and effect is even more lamentable; one loses the level path, becoming mired in darkness and madness.
When the time comes to personally undergo the bitter retribution, only then will one realize that the karma of good and evil is difficult to forget.
Vast and boundless, it invites calamity and misfortune. Evil is not reformed, nor is goodness cultivated. Without awakening and without delusion, every opening of the mouth is right;
before reaching the Niraya hell, one can hardly find rest.

Abandoning existence for the sickness of emptiness is likewise; turning one's back on emptiness to grasp at existence is just the same. The alms bowl and bag were brought while the night was still far from over;
Old Lu saw only the sharp point of the awl.
It is like avoiding drowning by throwing oneself into fire; though water and fire differ, how can their harm be distinguished?
If one enters a wild field and gathers what comes to hand, one need not move a step to return home.

Abandoning the deluded mind, one attempts to use the mind to eliminate delusion, yet delusion becomes even deeper. To realize that delusion is itself the truth is to see that "truth" does not exist as a thing.
A single strand of hemp thread and two needles;
to grasp at the truth is like a piece of shell or a tiny scale—it is not beautiful. A wooden woman pierces the clouds, laughing without ceasing. The great ocean...
Red dust rises from the bottom of the sea;

the mind of grasping and rejecting becomes artful and deceitful. One must know that truth and falsehood do not differ in their nature; practicing the Way to its ultimate realization is like half-extinguishing and half-arousing it.
It is still like climbing a tree to gaze upon the lotus.
The student fails to understand and thus practices; if one understands, how could practice be false?
To mistake the echo in a jar for the sound of a bell is not only devoid of reality, but is also self-deception.
Deeply convinced, one mistakes the thief for a son; love and delusion entangle the mind, and one does not realize it oneself. Wait until the year is exhausted and you shall see for yourself:
who will inherit the ancestral estate at this desolate source?
One squanders the wealth of the Dharma and abandons one's own merit; wandering through the three realms of suffering, what can one rely upon? Realization arises in a single kṣaṇa;
there is no need for arduous toil to gain benefit.
When merit has been extinguished, what further cause for suspicion is there? Five serve as gateways and one acts as a matchmaker;
from of old, the place of treasure has had no bolts or keys, yet it is simply that people of this age refuse to come.
There is nothing that does not arise from this mind, intellect, and consciousness. Though we have cohabited since time immemorial like bitter enemies, today we share a single household;
its boundless treasures shall no longer be stolen.

Therefore, in the Chan gate, one brings the mind to its ultimate end; with a steady and unswerving presence, one passes day and night. When Buddhas and Patriarchs gaze upon one another, they meet on the same path;
in great heat they welcome the cool, and in cold they face the sun.
Suddenly entering the power of the knowledge and vision of non-arising—how can this knowledge and vision of non-arising be discussed?
At times, gazing at the moon deep into the night, I have traveled to distant villages seeking alms.
A great man, majestic yet loving; like grass bowing before the wind, he moves without obstruction.
He serves as a model for both the wise and the ignorant, and those on perilous and evil paths rely upon him.
Wielding the sword of wisdom, frost and ice are cold; who in the world dares look directly upon it? Raising one's eyebrows, one returns at once:
behind Skull Peak, the grass stretches vast and deep.
The sharpness of Prajñā is like the flame of a vajra; firm and fierce, it can burn away the forest of delusive appearances. Sweeping all away, not even a hair’s breadth remains.
Only those standing by can laugh at this "old woman’s heart."
Not only can he crush the minds of the non-Buddhists; how could one ever count those who wear basins on their heads and plates upon their bellies?
When he sits upon the Vulture Peak and merely flicks his whip, the fine horses that follow the wind turn back of their own accord.

Long ago you already struck terror into the hearts of the celestial Māras; the relative strength of the heterodox and the orthodox can thus be known. It is simply that you, my followers, harbor heavy attachments of aversion and affection;
it is not that the Son of the Buddha lacks compassion.
Thundering the Dharma-thunder, a single strike resounds across the nine realms. Do not say that from the beginning there has been no form or image;
all sentient beings have had their eyes opened at once.
Beating the Dharma-drum, this is the direct standard for the Western Heaven and this land. It is only because the deluded sleep so heavily that they do not hear it themselves; it is not otherwise.
Avalokiteśvara’s mind is not yet all-pervasive;

he spreads the clouds of compassion and sprinkles the nectar of immortality. Between the human realm and the heavens, not even a speck of dust remains; in this vast mist, there is but one flavor, free from distinction.
It washes forth ten thousand kinds of new sprouts.
The treading of the dragon-elephants brings boundless moisture; moving with sovereign ease in all directions, may you never be fettered.
Until all sentient beings have fully realized Bodhi, I shall never lightly depart from the shore of affliction.
The three vehicles and five natures are all awakened; when unfolded they differ, but when rolled up they are the same.
Swallows, sparrows, peacocks, and phoenixes fly each in their own way, yet in the end none depart from empty space.

The snow mountains are lush and pure, free from all impurity; with timely rain and timely wind, their roots remain hidden. Do not say that because it flows on continuously there is nothing of consequence;
its message has already been conveyed to the descendants of the King.
I always receive the pure *tathāgata-garbha* (pure *sudhā*); were it not for a precious vessel, it would be difficult to store. Who in all the world knows this flavor?
Hanshan claps his hands and laughs at Fenggan.
The single nature perfectly penetrates all natures; this nature is vast and enduring, such that one is many.
If you understand that one and many are neither identical nor different, will you be able to realize that there is no coming or meeting between identity and difference?
A single dharma universally contains all dharmas; one dharma acts as the host while the many act as guests. Where there is neither host nor guest, that itself is the host-guest relationship.
A mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru does not obstruct anyone.
The full moon universally manifests in all waters; neither near nor far, its essence is eternally constant.
Its reflections divide and depart toward south, north, east, and west, yet it stands tall beyond the heavens with light that remains in abundance.

All waters and moons are encompassed within a single moon; the moon does not divide its form, nor do the waters remain solitary. People of this age have not yet penetrated the path of the clear waves;
they merely say that the cold radiance fills the great void.
The Dharmakāya of all Buddhas enters my own nature; Without self or person, I treat the holy and the common alike.
On the secluded path, fallen flowers are red as fire; Around the gate, flowing water is blue as indigo.
My nature returns to merge with the Tathāgata; the place of merging is neither another nor myself. An iron ship sinks atop the summit of Mount Sumeru;
an ear-pierced barbarian monk snaps his fingers in the dark.
The first bhūmi is fully endowed with all bhūmis; the distinctions of stages and practices reside within this very body.
Having traversed the three great kalpas of asaṃkhyeya aeons, this year’s poverty is just like last year’s.
Neither form nor mind, neither karma nor action; all such conceptual proliferation and words are utterly inadequate.
Only the Retired Scholar Pan of Mount Hua, while gazing and chanting on the road, rode backward upon his donkey.

In a single snap of the fingers, eighty thousand gateways are perfectly realized; these eighty thousand Dharma-gateways reside in a single place. If one is deluded regarding this single place, one wanders in vain pursuit;
yet if this single place is illuminated, there is no further basis for reliance.
In a single instant, three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are extinguished; in one thought-moment there is no arising, and even "one" does not exist.
When the great earth is entirely identical to the *Rūpya-dhātu*, what divergent paths could there be that do not return to the same destination?
All numerical phrases and non-numerical phrases, with their myriad names categorized by nature and characteristics— shut the door and claim only that the sky has not yet dawned,
unaware that the sun has risen outside the gate.
What connection has this with my spiritual awakening? The true mechanism of the thousand sages is not easily encountered. The Bagua of Mingzhou is full of madness and strangeness;
amidst the clamor, he constantly holds it up to show those on the path.
It cannot be disparaged; the majesty of the celestial armies and the Māra-queen is but a hollow beauty. Where the light of compassion shines, all turn to take refuge.
Beholding oneself in the clear mirror, one feels shame and remorse.
It cannot be praised; even empty space has never known separation from stillness. In the cave of Subhūti, not a blade of grass grows. Kauśika—
In vain one scatters heavenly flowers;
its essence is like empty space, without shore or limit. The subtle words of the secret treasury cannot be fully explained;
even the Ten Sages and Three Worthies do not know its whereabouts. At times it hangs idly before the temple gate.

Without leaving its original place, it is eternally serene; it is neither sentient being nor Buddha. Suddenly, one knocks down Mount Sumeru, and only then does one believe that from the beginning there has never been a single thing.
Seeking, you know that you cannot see him; not seeing, you must return by this path. The sick bird dwells only beneath the reed leaves;
the swift falcon, as soon as it rises, soars across the heavens.
It cannot be grasped; clouds arise and lightning flashes as the world turns black. Linji returns empty-handed from his journey, yet he is stubbornly called a "white-handed thief.
It cannot be let go; it fills and permeates the four quarters and the zenith and nadir. How could Śāriputra know this when he wished to cast it aside? He needlessly incurs [reproach].
Celestial flowers fill the lapels of his robes;
they cannot be grasped, yet here they are. Without leaves or roots, they grow everywhere. Yesterday, as the curtain was drawn, they passed with the rain;
today, on the road, they obstruct the traveler’s path.
Speaking in silence, illuminating within the darkness; when light and dark are forgotten, all becomes as level as a whetstone.
This is the ultimate place where the Dharma-gate of Non-duality is expounded, sounding like thunder within the city of Vaiśālī.
When speaking, he remained silent; he cut off all causal connections. Only when he retracted his tongue could he begin to explain. For forty-nine years there was not a single word;
how then could the Dragon Palace or the Ocean Treasury transmit it?
The gate of great giving stands open without obstruction; one neither loathes the flowing spring nor craves the mountain.
Facing dust and ashes, with hair like snow, one passes through the Tongguan Pass on foot or horseback.
Someone asked me which school I followed; without sparing my eyebrows, I briefly explained: Clouds arise on the eastern ridge, while the western ridge turns white;
Flowers bloom on the front mountain, while the back mountain turns red.
Proclaiming the power of the Mahāprajñā: the true secret of the Buddhas of past and present. Xie San was originally a fisherman;
having caught the stream, he sought no further trace.
Whether it be right or wrong, people do not recognize it; they do not know who this person truly is.
Changing faces and altering heads like an illusion—[blank] [blank] [blank] [blank] in the midst of the ordinary.
Moving against or with the current, the heavens cannot fathom it; there is no further ritual model or rule to serve as a guide. How could one ever exhaust the boundaries of the yellow earth?
It is in vain that one uses a broken awl to probe its depth.
I have long since practiced through many kalpas; through such cultivation, I have realized the power of non-arising. The deluded person seeks the Way but does not practice;
it is like steaming sand in the hope that it will become food.
This is not a casual deception; from the beginning, how could truth and falsehood ever interfere with one another? How many have donned tiger skins while possessing the nature of sheep?
To recognize true gold, one must look within the fire.
Erecting the Dharma Banner: The model of Vulture Peak is peerless. A girl with her hair bound in a topknot wears a straw hat;
carrying a *khakkhara* staff in hand, she crosses the cold river.
Establishing the School’s Tenet: Who can entrust themselves to the left hollow and the right unevenness? When the boatman of Hai-men passed through Yangzhou, he had eight arms.
Nata is as cunning as a ghost;
clearly, Caoxi is the Buddha’s command. Wherever one is, that is Caoxi. Day after day the sun rises from the eastern side;
morning after morning the rooster cries at the fifth watch.
The first Kāśyapa was the foremost transmitter of the lamp; he wore rag robes from refuse heaps and knew contentment within himself.
Yet, because he broke into a dance and leaked his celestial secret, he has suffered [retribution] until the present day.
The Record of the Twenty-Eighth Patriarch of the Western Heaven: No longer lingering in secluded crags, he entered the dust of the world together.
A single staff, free from knots or blemishes, He earnestly entrusted to the traveler at night.
Entering this land, he responded to the conditions of faith; the blossoming of the five-leaf flower—how could it be by chance? Without a sage, all is vast and empty, a state no one can comprehend.
For nine years he sat alone, his nose reaching toward the heavens.
Bodhidharma was the First Patriarch; in vain do they say he came from the West wishing to transmit the robe. Yet I admire the King of Liang’s true magnanimity:
chasing him across the cold river, he allowed no turning back.

The transmission of the robe through six generations was heard throughout the world; to manifest the Dharma, I shall briefly record the essential principle. At that time, let go completely without error;
why is it that when people come, they cannot lift it up?
The number of those who attain the Way in later generations is infinite; it is not only from beyond the ridges that they come.
One must believe that the spring sun reaches all things, so that flowers and trees, high and low, bloom all at once.
In truth, nothing is established. The white colt is no more swift than the flowing waves. On that day, King Wen recognized the treasure;
Bian He is laughable for shedding tears in vain. Delusion is fundamentally empty.
The traveler yearns for home as the year draws to a close; every step taken is home, and one need only return. Why labor?
A lingering resentment flows toward the western wind.

Both existence and non-existence are cast aside, yet it is not a mere emptiness. If one wishes to preserve emptiness, it remains an obstruction. After the mountain man has departed, the aged ape cries;
when the thatched hut is empty, the white clouds remain.
The twenty gates of emptiness have never attached themselves; the lingering illness of truth and falsehood has been removed. A single building stands where clouds reach, and no person arrives;
thousands of crags and ten thousand ravines encircle my thatched cottage.
The single nature of the Tathāgata’s essence is inherently identical; within this identity, there is no path, whether one goes west or east. The shrimp at the bottom of the well blows its war horn;
the pillar before the gate laughs at the lantern.
The mind is the root. Darkly soaring and slantingly coiling, its traces are already revealed. Alas, those who look directly downward do not see it;
they vainly pass on branches and leaves to their descendants.
Phenomena are dust. The moment a single point arises, one loses the truth. Do not say that within names there is no substantial meaning—how much confusion!
The original body is fully revealed;

these two kinds [of phenomena] are like blemishes upon a mirror. They obscure the luminous spirit, resembling mental impurities; yet within the mountains, rivers, and great earth, there is not a single thread of obstruction.
Who hangs [the image] upon the high terrace to distinguish beauty from ugliness?

When stains and blemishes are completely removed, the light finally appears. The solitary radiance is revealed alone, chilling the great chiliocosm. When free from dust, even the transmission of robe and bowl is not permitted;
one must know that playing with shadows is not easily observed.
When both mind and dharmas are forgotten, the nature is itself the truth. This true nature is neither non-existent nor existent. At Shaolin, how many times was it pondered in vain!
Vimalakīrti did not dare to lightly open his mouth.
Alas for the Dharma of the Final Age! Turning one's back on the true wind, beings encounter all things in a state of delusion like ignorant children.
They stand in vain outside the burning house with its three carts; when will they together reach the crossroads?
This is an evil age, close to the three calamities; though one calls out to sentient beings afflicted by defilements, they do not turn back.
The myriad sufferings of war and famine are all created by the human mind.

Sentient beings of meager merit are difficult to discipline; they rush headlong with treacherous crookedness like leaping monkeys. The trees on the bank are about to collapse as the fish have little water.
Alas! They do not realize the words of those of old.
The Sage has long been gone and false views run deep; the fetters of self-conceit entangle us, obscuring the true Buddha. How much toil has the Compassionate Guide endured to deliver us!
Having briefly emerged from the river of craving, we sink back into it once more.
When Mara is strong and the Dharma weak, there is much enmity and harm. Though good and evil differ, the Buddha-nature is the same. It is well to clarify one's own self at this time;
the light and shadow of a hundred years turn empty in the blink of an eye.
Hearing the teaching of the Tathāgata’s sudden (sudden) gate, half-smiling and half-angry, my heart was not pleased.
One morning, returning to see my compassionate parent, I finally realized that from of old we shared the same family vocation.
Regretfully, I fail to extinguish it and shatter the tile; in empty truth and signlessness, I vainly consult the stars.
The ant is laughable for failing to gauge its own strength, wishing to stir a slight breeze to shake a great pillar.
The action is formed within the mind; how great a mistake! It is like using a golden pellet to chase after a flying sparrow;
the master of ignorance indulges in greed and anger, exhausting the family wealth without realizing it at all.

The calamity rests upon one's own person; it is difficult to escape. Reaching this point, it serves only to distinguish the foolish from the wise. There are a million kinds of agonizing pain and chilling misery;
though father and son are close, they cannot substitute for one another.
There is no need for resentment or to blame others; it is simply that one's own wisdom is not clear, resulting in delusion and obstruction.
Awakening and affliction have long been without root; they depend only upon a single moment of turning the mind.
If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, consider how the retribution for such cruel offenses is truly unbearable;
it is not only those who slander the Dharma who sink alone into this abyss, but the six thieves that endanger humanity must also be guarded against.
Do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata. The suffering resulting from the causes and conditions of withholding the Dharma is difficult to fathom;
even if one passes through empty kalpas dwelling in other realms, when this world-system is formed again, one shall return to undergo it.
The Sandalwood Grove: Looking out as far as the eye can see, a solitary path winds deep within. How many times have travelers heard its fragrance strike their nostrils?
Yet in an instant, they lose their original mind. There are no other trees;
leaf by leaf, branch by branch, all share the rain and dew. The traveler scorched by heat calls out, but cannot return. Thus it is through the four seasons.
Vastly it spreads a canopy of green shade;
dense, profound, and solemn, the lion dwells here. Lifting his eyes, he lofts a hundred-fathom majesty; his traces do not allow others to be seen beyond the forest.
What else could possibly find its way back into this place?

Wandering alone in the stillness of the forest, he neither abides, nor moves, nor leans upon anything. When his golden fur merely brushes against the ground, boundless pure breezes follow his every step.
The running beasts and flying birds all fled far away; looking in the four directions, all was silent and the realm was empty.
Was it that he had never had companions from of old? It was simply because their fur and colors were not the same.
The lion cub exerts its full majesty—how marvelous! Entering the cave to hide its body, it alone attains the sublime.
From the beginning, it has not permitted the elephant king to know its whereabouts.
As the multitude follows behind, its tusks and claws can no longer be concealed; its power is already established. It plays through the empty mountains with many guises, then performs a somersault.
In a single cast, there is neither new nor old;
at three years of age, he was already able to let out a great roar. His lineage is without distinction and his power is complete;
he sits cutting off the paths of east and west. Majestic and towering, he remains forever before the green crags.
If a jackal pursues the Dharma King, wandering in vain through the forests and by the mountain slopes, it merely deceives itself by borrowing the tiger’s majesty;
as soon as it encounters its true nature, it is struck with terror.
For a hundred years, demons have opened their mouths in vain; when wisdom is extinguished and the body reduced to ashes, what leisure can there be?
How does this compare to the shade beneath the tree in the Lumbinī Garden, where, upon birth, he looked in the four directions, forever beyond all pursuit?
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching: The dragon has emerged from the sea, no longer confined by its cage; as soon as the thunderclap roars, the rain pours down.
Countless beings among devas and humans awaken from their dreams.
Do not rely on human sentiments; if you cling to human sentiments, the Way will not be realized. How petty is the Old State Official of Nanyang! He merely treads...

Walking upon the crown of Vairocana’s head, if there is doubt that cannot be resolved, one must simply strive for clarity. Whether true or false, one must leave behind all afflictions; throughout the day, the ancient path calls out to people to walk it.
Alas, those deluded disciples are unable to resist their attachment to the wild weeds.
It is not that this mountain monk seeks to assert self over others; it is precisely at this time that I would forget my own body for the sake of the Dharma.
If one does not brandish the blade of wisdom against deviant forces, who will know of the flawless jewel within the topknot?
In practicing the Way, one fears falling into the pit of nihilism or eternalism; once fallen into this pit, it is difficult to escape.
This morning the drums were beaten for the three armies, yet when the weapons were brandished, they were not what was expected.
Neither "not" nor "not-not. Look at the spiritual sprout before it has yet emerged. When the great garuḍa spreads its wings, it brushes the clouds and mists;
who would deign to learn from the cold cicada that clings to a dying branch?
Is it so? Or is it not? The western neighbor has taken possession of the eastern neighbor’s land. If the tree at the center belongs to you, there is no need for further effort.
Seeking the four boundaries point by point—missing it by a hair’s breadth is to lose a thousand li.
It is not that they fail to interact with one another, but rather that they obscure their own spiritual essence. A spark of stone, once flicked, vanishes beyond the heavens;
yet the deluded person still gazes toward the stars at the edge of the moon.

This is precisely the dragon girl’s sudden attainment of Buddhahood; her cultivation did not require passing through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. People today are lamentably lost in delusion and falsehood;
though the sun reaches the southern solstice, they do not even know it themselves.

It was not that Shanxing fell into ruin at birth; he simply forgot cause and effect and lost his right understanding. Among the lineage of a Wheel-Turning King, there is no distinction of high or low;
why then should death and rebirth diverge along different paths?
Since my early years, I have accumulated learning; I have long lamented that every moment is fleeting and difficult to retain.
Like the continuous flow of a cold mountain stream, it will not cease until it reaches the vast blue ocean.

I have also once investigated commentaries and sought out the sūtras and śāstras; I cherish the thought that this work shall serve as a lamp to shatter the darkness of the age. In my fervent aspiration, I wish to exhaust the meanings of the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
yet how could I have known that "non-explanation" (avaktavya) is the true vehicle?
Discriminating names and forms, one knows no rest; it is like gazing at the sun through clouds. When appearances are exhausted and names vanish, the Truth is shown to you:
New Roach pepper and lacquer from Ginzhou.
Entering the sea to count its sands is but a futile exhaustion; it is precisely this state of being "awake" that becomes increasingly unbearable.
Only Mañjuśrī knows this number: three times three before, and three times three after.
Yet one is harshly rebuked by the Tathāgata: "When will your running and seeking after external things ever cease?
Though the priceless jewel within your robe exists, alas, you remain muddled and intoxicated, yet to awaken."
What benefit is there in counting the treasures of others, while one’s own household wealth is being cast aside?
If you can take it up with both hands and put it to use, there is no need for the hardship of wandering through mountains and rivers.
In the past, stumbling along, I realized my journey was in vain; I traveled all the way from the southern heavens to the northern heavens.
Time and again, by the side of clear waters and green mountains, I encountered the Patriarchs, yet I did not recognize them.
For many years I have vainly been a traveler in the dust and wind; on my departure, not even half of my clothes remained. Though the old garden is but a few paces away, I have yet to return;
my compassionate parents stand in vain at their door as the sun slants down.
If one's spiritual disposition is perverse and one further encounters a false teacher, the illness will only intensify.
However, if one meets a true *kalyāṇamitra*, even withered wood will sprout flowers.

Erroneous understanding—wherein knowledge becomes an obstruction and comprehension becomes a hindrance—is like realizing that floating flowers in space were never produced in the first place; though they appear profusely, they are empty.
In their actions, they harbor neither hatred nor love;
they fail to comprehend the Tathāgata’s perfect and sudden discipline, instead vying with one another over emptiness and existence. Like the Duke of Ye who loved paintings, they are just like this:
as soon as they see a true dragon, they are struck with alarm.

The diligence of the Two Vehicles does not equal the Bodhicitta; seeking liberation through the realization of partial emptiness, the children of the three realms are daily consumed by fire, yet they refuse to turn their minds toward compassion and wisdom.
The heterodox teachers are clever but lack true wisdom; they harbor preferences in their hearts and cannot let them go for even a moment.
Yang Zhu only laments the many diverging paths, unaware that beneath his feet lies his own home.

They are likewise deluded; rising and sitting like wooden puppets, they follow their ancestral livelihoods from generation to generation, never realizing that even their straw sandals are worn through.

They are also somewhat foolish, for when confronted with impermanence at every turn, they respond only with hatred or attachment, spending their time piling up sand and dirt as if practicing siege warfare. Alas for you!
Who would have known that the universe is so vast?
From an empty fist pointing upward, true understanding arises. Those of deluded, petty, and frantic ignorance are dark-witted;
yet if one realizes this mind has nothing to be attained, then the spring breeze and autumn moon are naturally serene and sparse.

To grasp the finger and mistake it for the moon is to labor in vain; not only do you lose the moon, but you remain deluded by the finger itself. Suddenly, when the moon is seen, the finger is forgotten;
within its cold radiance, the myriad phenomena of the universe appear in their full splendor.
Within the dharmas of the faculties and their objects, one falsely fabricates monstrosities; as shadows and phenomena entwine, right cultivation is obscured.
It is laughable that a magician, encountering illusory objects, looks upon them with doubt and terror, unable to find rest.
Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata. Spring arrives and the myriad flowers bloom through the rain.
Those who cannot discern whether this is form or mind strike the bell and beat the drum atop the high terrace.
Only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara; able to contemplate like the moon that has not forgotten its radiance.
If you wish to know that all phenomena are fundamentally boundless, the great earth, mountains, and rivers are the eyes.
Upon realization, karmic obstacles are fundamentally empty; all phenomena are rootless, being merely false discriminations. When the mind arises, it is the time that phenomena arise;
if the mind does not arise, phenomena naturally cease.
If one has not yet realized it, one must still repay past debts; why doubt the golden needles and the horse-barley? Who says that the Patriarchs and Buddhas have no place to escape?
Even if one were to sacrifice their entire body daily, they would still remain unaware.
Encountering a royal feast while hungry, one cannot eat; high and low minds arise and create estrangement among themselves.
If even those summoned for food behave thus, alas, how many are there who die of hunger!
When the sick encounter the King of Physicians, how could they fail to be healed? Though the medicine and the illness are suddenly eliminated, the fish-trap has not yet been forgotten.
How does this compare to the "poisoned drum," where a single beat causes all who lie listening or pass by to fall into profound stillness?

Practicing dhyāna amidst desire through the power of knowledge and vision, one dwells in the dust all day long yet remains free from dust. To settle the mind, there is no need to distinguish between the city and the wilds;
wherever one treads upon the eyebrows, that is the truth.
A lotus born from fire can never be destroyed; its flowers resemble Mount Sumeru, and its leaves are like space.
It scatters its pure fragrance throughout the three realms, having no anxiety about falling easily before the western wind.
Vīradatta committed a grave offense yet awakened to non-arising; good and evil have never been confused from the outset. When the clouds of the five aggregates disperse, the moon fills the sky;
there is no need to further inquire about the path home.
He attained Buddhahood long ago and remains present until now; his marks and signs are majestic in a hundred thousand ways.
If you do not understand what is proclaimed from his golden mouth, try searching beneath the seven-pound hempen robe.
The Lion’s Roar: Thirty-three people all fled in terror; the painted vase was broken, yet they returned.
The green mountains and flowing waters remain as they were before.
Fearless One, you speak directly to drive out the nails of the deluded; let the old man by the stream not knit his brows. Summer has come.
The blazing glow brings snow even in winter;
I deeply lament this ignorant and stubborn hide. My native land is not far, yet I am unwilling to cross over; I resemble a floating duckweed whose roots and stem have been severed.
Adrift in the cycle of birth and death, I trust myself to the winds and waves.

Knowing only that committing grave offenses obstructs Bodhi, they fail to realize that the nature of sin is like waves arising from frozen ice. The deluded person dies of thirst without lowering their head;
how could they recognize that the solid ice is entirely water?
Failing to see the Tathāgata’s secret key, who would dare to proclaim it? The pierced-eared barbarian monk will surely laugh aloud;
it is as clear as snow upon which frost is added.

There were two bhikṣus who had committed sexual misconduct and murder; they were ashamed to have their names listed among the superior beings of the Golden Field. In their terror, they did not know what their minds should do;
wishing to rely on the pure precepts to save their remaining lives.
Upāli, the glow of the firefly increases the bonds of sin; weighing the light and heavy, one must analyze them down to the finest hair’s breadth.
Piteous indeed is the frantic heart, yet though it is urgent, it remains unaware that fish are swimming beneath its feet.
The Great Being Vimalakīrti suddenly dispels all doubt; in the three realms, there is no mind—briefly and lightly established.
The man from the borderlands seizes the young qilin and releases it into the Jeta Grove, where it can no longer be found.
Just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow, and when the frost and snow have vanished, the springtime is revealed— Who,
at the place where Lingyun opened his eyes, recognized the old master of the peach blossoms?
Inconceivable! To attempt to measure it is in vain; good and evil have no source, for its nature is fundamentally eternal. Fragrant Son Xiangyan opens his mouth in vain;
when he lifts his foot, how could he ever recognize the site of enlightenment?
The power of liberation is like a high wind: without shadow or form, it penetrates all points of contact;
ten thousand miles of floating clouds dissolve away, leaving a single bright moon in the cold sky.

The wondrous function is as boundless as the sands of the Ganges; having encountered you for a brief moment due to deep karmic conditions from the past, I now reflect that the day of true transformation has not yet been cleansed, and how many times I have wandered like a drifting gourd.
I venture to decline the toil of the fourfold offerings; it is like feeding a donkey or a horse—picking up from the edge of the trough to fill a bowl.
Who in the four seas would dare to set a price for this?
Even ten thousand taels of gold could not repay it; this heart of gratitude is ultimately difficult to describe.
Even if one were to bestow treasures as numerous as grains of sand, it would still not equal a single point of grace from Caoxi.

Even grinding one's bones to dust would not suffice as recompense; in vain do people speak of heaven and earth, or dew and rain. Throughout antiquity and today, who has been a person capable of repaying this kindness?
If there is even a single thread of attachment, one has already failed them.
A single phrase clearly transcends ten billion worlds; as for discussing this single phrase, I have no ability. Such a proclamation clarifies the fundamental principle:
it brings to laughter the blue-eyed monk who came from the West.
The King of Dharmas is none other than this very one. The ten bodies and three bodies are not merely similar; they possess a numinous light that illuminates both past and present.
Why must the *svastika* be inscribed upon the breast?
The most supreme and victorious. If one were to proclaim it, the Vulture Peak and Shaoshi Mountain would all be empty echoes. The Child of Silence can proclaim it;
come, come, and I shall refund you the money for your straw sandals.
The Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have all together witnessed this; there is no other dharma to be transmitted or upheld.
It is where the bright moon first rises over the ocean and sky, and when the cries of the gibbons in the cliffside trees have just ceased.
I now understand this wish-fulfilling jewel; its brilliant radiance has no front or back. Now I cast it before the assembly;
yet if you hesitate or deliberate, you shall not see it.
Those who receive it with faith all attain resonance. Laughing, he enters the thousand peaks without turning his head. After the meal, two or three cups of mountain tea;
the Buddhas and Patriarchs as numerous as dust motes are all but drifting away.
Clearly seen—what more is there to say? All things are ever new as another year passes. Departing and departing, yet not returning—where can one find peace?
Deeply locked away at the edge of the severed clouds.
Not a single thing remains. □□□. □□□□ the kalpa-fire burns it away. Though King Yue may have had the power to topple the state of Wu, Fan Li’s solitary boat cannot easily be summoned.
There is no person either; there is only empty space as an old neighbor. Illusion perishes and illusion arises, yet neither exists—where else could one seek the distant or the kin?
There is no Buddha either; the ancients needlessly descended into the lair of the black dragon. To speak of the marks and signs being cultivated for a hundred kalpas is in vain. The red furnace...
Things cannot remain within the flames.
The great chiliocosm and its myriad worlds are but bubbles upon the sea; arising and ceasing leave no trace—who is their master? Xuefeng once showed this to the assembly:
"Ten thousand miles of cloudless sky, the sun at high noon."
All worthy sages are like lightning brushed away; their forms are nameless. The sky is empty, the sun and moon are there, and people return to the mouth [of discourse].
How many times has one grasped the "blowing-hair" sword, yet it remains not level?
Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon one’s crown, one would spontaneously follow conditions without acting;
though fire consumes and wind shakes all things until they are empty, no one has ever seen the blue sky fall or crumble.

When concentration and wisdom are perfectly clear and bright, one never loses them; able to withstand worldly toil, their essence is inherently eternal. Throughout past and present, there is no place of increase or decrease;
people of old have merely used this as a metaphor for the vajra.
The sun may grow cold; how could true gold ever again become ore? The demonic artisan cannot apply his bellows to it;
for ten thousand ages, my heart remains tirelessly vigilant.

The moon may grow hot; this body is like space, neither severed nor extinguished. It is only through human delusion that its waning and waxing are perceived; beyond the heavens, [it remains as it is].
The solitary light never ceases;
no host of māras can destroy this true teaching. This true teaching remains evergreen like a cypress in the courtyard.
How many times have we seen the snow and frost wither ten thousand trees, yet the tree that soars into the void and towers above the balustrade remains even more verdant?
The elephant carriage advances laboriously upon the rugged path; the true body is like space, unimpeded by anything.
When the clouds have cleared from Mount Fusang and the sun has already risen, what need is there to wait for the flickering torchlight that never ceases?
Who has seen a cicada able to block a carriage track? In an instant it is crushed to pieces, yet its intent remains fierce. Alas, you are not as fortunate as the cicada that relies on the tree;
drinking dew and singing in the wind, it passes its entire life.
The great elephant does not roam upon the rabbit’s path; the shattering of partiality and the dismantling of the small are not in vain.
If one can enter the path within non-existence, the golden locks and the profound gate will all be cast aside.
One who has attained great enlightenment is not constrained by minor details; those who merely mimic the mind of a realized practitioner are ridiculed by the enlightened.
If one’s deportment lacks the grace of Xi Zi, to imitate her frown only brings further ugliness—this is truly pitiable.

Do not slander the vast blue sky with your narrow, biased views. Though the leaking pipe may reach its end, how could the heavens be small? When the mind and wisdom are opened and clarified, false perceptions vanish;
only then does one know that the Dharma-realm has no boundaries.
I have not yet fully explained it; let me now resolve it for you. This meaning is clear and cannot be easily transmitted.
Who would be willing to return beneath the ancient crags? Let the blue seas change into mulberry fields as they may.
Now, the Dharma cannot be seen, heard, perceived, or known; yet seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing are not external to the Dharma.

To be deluded regarding it is to be an ordinary person; to comprehend it is to be a sage. Therefore, those of old who attained the Way were neither identical with nor separate from it, neither bound nor liberated.
To manifest function in accordance with capacity, it is inevitable that one must speak; yet in its sovereign freedom, though one speaks all day long, one has never spoken at all.
In the past, when Yongjia met the Sixth Patriarch, he stood there shaking his staff, and the Way was present through direct perception.

He stayed for a single night, whereupon the Master composed for him the *Song of Certifying the Way*. The Way is fundamentally without certification; to certify it by means of a song, though not entirely avoidable, is nonetheless a matter of expedient expression.
Regarding these words, in the end there is nothing that binds them. Thus, those of later generations have attained awakening through his songs;
the number of those who have so awakened is beyond measure. Furthermore, the number of those who have subsequently composed commentaries upon them is likewise beyond measure.
Yet, those who have truly captured the essence of Yongjia’s spirit are, it seems, rare indeed. This is Master Chan Master Quan.
His brilliance surpassed his peers. In the intervals between the lines of his songs, while he was leading his disciples at Qianqing, he composed verses (*śloka*).

For the most part, he spoke of emptiness through form; he spoke of wisdom within meditative concentration. Without perceiving a single characteristic, he was fully present throughout the Dharma-realm;
without departing from a single speck of dust, he perfectly possessed the Buddha-nature. His phrasing was elegant and free-flowing, and his intent was vast and profound. It was luminous.
It is manifest. That the mind of Yongjia was awakened after a period of desolation spanning several hundred years is something for which I am personally fortunate;
having been able to inquire into the Master’s legacy and thereby attain enlightenment, I have looked upon his verses with admiration for his pure style, unable to restrain myself.

I have therefore commissioned them to be carved onto printing blocks to broaden their dissemination, hoping that those who are obstructed may find passage and those in darkness may find clarity, so that all may become one.
That I attained sudden enlightenment through transcendence is the gift of my teacher.
Written on the tenth day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Xining era. By Zhu Kuang of Kuocang. Postscript.
